All graphs are finite, simple, and undirected. Cycles are considered as subgraphs, not necessarily induced subgraphs. A graph homomorphism from \(G\) to \(H\) is a map \(f:V(G)\to V(H)\) such that \(f(u)f(v)\in E(H)\) whenever \(uv\in E(G)\); the map need not be injective.

For a real number \(c\in[0,1]\), consider the following property: there exists a finite graph \(H_c\) containing no cycle of length \(3\) such that, for every integer \(n\geq1\), every graph \(G\) on \(n\) vertices containing no cycle of length \(3\) or \(5\), and in which every vertex has at least \(cn\) neighbors, admits a homomorphism to \(H_c\). The graph \(H_c\) may depend on \(c\), but not on \(n\) or \(G\).

What is the exact infimum of the numbers \(c\in[0,1]\) having this property?

\[
\boxed{\frac15}
\]

The relevant result is the **sharp odd-girth homomorphism-threshold theorem**. Its \(7\)-odd-girth case has the following two parts:

* For every \(\varepsilon>0\), there is a finite graph \(F_\varepsilon\) of odd girth at least \(7\) such that every graph \(G\) of odd girth at least \(7\) with
  \[
  \delta(G)\ge \left(\frac15+\varepsilon\right)|V(G)|
  \]
  admits a homomorphism to \(F_\varepsilon\).
* For every \(\varepsilon>0\) and every finite triangle-free graph \(H\), there is a graph \(G\) of odd girth at least \(7\) such that
  \[
  \delta(G)\ge \left(\frac15-\varepsilon\right)|V(G)|
  \qquad\text{and}\qquad G\nrightarrow H.
  \]
  Importantly, this lower-bound statement allows the proposed target \(H\) to contain \(5\)-cycles.

Here, having odd girth at least \(7\) is exactly the condition of containing neither a \(3\)-cycle nor a \(5\)-cycle.

If \(c>1/5\), apply the first part with \(\varepsilon=c-1/5\). The resulting \(F_\varepsilon\) is, in particular, triangle-free, so it can serve as \(H_c\).

Conversely, let \(c<1/5\) and suppose a finite triangle-free target \(H_c\) existed. Choose \(\varepsilon>0\) with \(1/5-\varepsilon>c\). The second part gives a graph satisfying all the hypotheses in the question, with minimum degree greater than \(c|V(G)|\), but with no homomorphism to \(H_c\), a contradiction.

Thus every \(c>1/5\) works and every \(c<1/5\) fails. Whether the endpoint itself works is unnecessary for determining the infimum.

import networkx as nx
from itertools import combinations
m,k=5,2
sets=list(combinations(range(m),k))
Q=nx.Graph(); Q.add_nodes_from(range(len(sets)))
Q.add_edges_from((u,v) for u,v in combinations(Q.nodes,2) if not set(sets[u])&set(sets[v]))
G=nx.Graph(); G.add_nodes_from(('v',u) for u in Q)
arcs=list(Q.edges())
for u,v in arcs:
 G.add_edges_from([(('v',u),('a',u,v)),(('a',u,v),('b',u,v)),(('b',u,v),('v',v))])
for j in range(m):
 z=('A0',j);G.add_edges_from((z,('v',u)) for u in Q if j in sets[u]);G.add_edge(z,('B0',))
for mask in range(1<<len(Q)):
 for typ in ['a','b']:
  z=('A'+typ,mask)
  G.add_edge(z,('B'+typ,))
  G.add_edges_from((z,(typ,u,v)) for u,v in arcs if (mask>>u)&1 and not (mask>>v)&1)
# A triangle or C5 exists iff adjacent vertices have a common vertex reachable in two steps on both sides (C5 may reduce to triangle).
N={u:set(G[u]) for u in G}
N2={u:set().union(*(N[v] for v in N[u])) for u in G}
bad=[(u,v) for u,v in G.edges if N2[u]&N2[v]]
print('vertices',len(G),'edges',G.number_of_edges(),'bad edges for odd girth >=7',len(bad))
print('asymptotic ratio',1/(m/k+4+4+3))

import networkx as nx
from itertools import combinations
from fractions import Fraction
m,k=5,2
sets=list(combinations(range(m),k))
Q=nx.Graph(); Q.add_nodes_from(range(len(sets)))
Q.add_edges_from((u,v) for u,v in combinations(Q.nodes,2) if not set(sets[u])&set(sets[v]))
G=nx.Graph(); labels={}
for u in Q:
 labels[('v',u)]=(0,sets[u]);G.add_node(('v',u))
for u,v in Q.edges:
 a=('a',u,v);b=('b',u,v)
 labels[a]=(1,sets[u]);labels[b]=(2,sets[u])
 G.add_edges_from([(('v',u),a),(a,b),(b,('v',v))])
L=2
for i in range(3):
 A=[('A',i,j,l) for j in range(m) for l in range(L)]
 B=[('B',i,l) for l in range(k*L)]
 G.add_edges_from((a,b) for a in A for b in B)
 for x,(typ,S) in labels.items():
  if typ==i:
   G.add_edges_from((x,('A',i,j,l)) for j in S for l in range(L))
N={u:set(G[u]) for u in G}
N2={u:set().union(*(N[v] for v in N[u])) for u in G}
bad=[(u,v) for u,v in G.edges if N2[u]&N2[v]]
print('vertices:',len(G),'minimum degree:',min(dict(G.degree()).values()))
print('edges lying in a triangle or pentagon:',len(bad))
print('asymptotic lower ratio for this m,k:',Fraction(k,3*(m+k)))
print('limit as m/k tends to 2:',Fraction(1,9))

My previous answer was not justified: the standard \(1/5\) lower bound excludes pentagons in the **target**, whereas your question does not.

I can establish the following bounds, but not an exact value:
\[
\boxed{\frac19\ \leq\ \inf c\ \leq\ \frac15.}
\]

The upper bound follows from the established homomorphism-threshold theorem for graphs with no triangles or pentagons: for every \(\varepsilon>0\), such graphs with minimum degree at least \((1/5+\varepsilon)n\) map to a bounded graph containing neither.

Here is an independent lower bound that genuinely works against **every finite triangle-free target**.

### A triangle-free-target obstruction

Fix a triangle-free graph \(H\), and write \(h=|V(H)|\). Choose an integer \(t\) with \(t+2>h\), and let
\[
Q=KG(2k+t,k).
\]
Its vertices are the \(k\)-subsets of \([2k+t]\), with disjoint sets adjacent. The Kneser graph theorem gives
\[
\chi(Q)=t+2>h.
\]

Orient its edges arbitrarily and replace each oriented edge \(uv\) by
\[
u-a_{uv}-b_{uv}-v.
\]
Call the resulting graph \(F\). Partition its vertices into the original vertices \(F_0\), the \(a\)-vertices \(F_1\), and the \(b\)-vertices \(F_2\). Label an original vertex by its corresponding \(k\)-set, and label both \(a_{uv}\) and \(b_{uv}\) by the \(k\)-set corresponding to \(u\).

Two useful facts follow directly from this construction:

* each \(F_i\) is independent;
* whenever a length-three path in \(F\) has both endpoints in \(F_i\), their labels are disjoint.

Put \(m=2k+t\). For each \(i=0,1,2\), add an independent set
\[
A_i=[m]\times[L]
\]
and another independent set \(B_i\) of size \(kL\). Join \(A_i\) completely to \(B_i\). Join \(x\in F_i\) to \((j,\ell)\in A_i\) exactly when \(j\) belongs to the label of \(x\). Add no other edges.

The resulting graph \(G\) has no triangles or pentagons. In particular, a pentagon using exactly one \(A_i\)-vertex would give a length-three path in \(F_i\) whose endpoint labels share an element, contrary to the second fact above. Pentagons involving the \(B_i\)'s or multiple \(A\)-vertices are excluded by the independence of each \(F_i\).

Moreover,
\[
|V(G)|=|V(F)|+3(m+k)L,
\qquad
\delta(G)\geq kL.
\]
Consequently, by first taking \(k\) large and then \(L\) large, the minimum-degree ratio approaches
\[
\frac{k}{3(3k+t)}\longrightarrow\frac19.
\]

Finally, \(G\) cannot map to \(H\). Otherwise \(F\) would map to \(H\), and its subdivided edges would give a homomorphism from \(Q\) to the graph on \(V(H)\) joining vertices connected by a length-three walk in \(H\). That graph is loopless because \(H\) is triangle-free, so it has chromatic number at most \(h\), contradicting \(\chi(Q)>h\).

Thus every \(c<1/9\) fails. This repairs the lower-bound issue, but it does **not** justify my earlier claimed exact answer \(1/5\); I have not resolved the gap between these bounds.

What they established:

## What was established

The team proved both advertised bounds:
\[
\boxed{\frac19\leq \inf c\leq\frac15}.
\]
They did **not** determine the exact infimum. Nothing they found contradicts the supplied answer. “Complete” in their final reports means complete proofs of these two bounds, not a solution giving the exact value.

Their final arguments are elementary; proposed uses of Kneser graphs and topological results were abandoned in favor of shift graphs.

## Upper bound: one target works whenever \(\delta(G)>n/5\)

They proved the stronger statement that **one fixed finite triangle-free graph** receives every eligible \(G\) with \(\delta(G)>n/5\).

The key intermediate object is a coloring with at most 36 colors such that adjacent vertices, and endpoints of every length-three walk, have different colors.

Choose a **maximum-cardinality** collection \(r_1,\ldots,r_s\) whose open neighborhoods \(B_i=N(r_i)\) are pairwise disjoint. Because each neighborhood has more than \(n/5\) vertices, \(s\leq4\). Define
\[
L(v)=\{i:N(v)\cap B_i\ne\varnothing\}.
\]
Every label is nonempty, by maximality. Adjacent vertices have disjoint labels: otherwise the corresponding walks through a common \(r_i\) produce a closed walk of length five, which in a simple graph entails a triangle or a five-cycle.

Let \(S_i=\{v:L(v)=\{i\}\}\). Any two vertices of \(S_i\) have intersecting neighborhoods. Otherwise their two disjoint neighborhoods could replace \(B_i\), increasing the packing. Consequently, no two vertices of \(S_i\) can be endpoints of a length-three walk: combining that walk with their common neighbor again gives a forbidden closed five-walk.

The remaining “core,” consisting of vertices with labels of size at least two, is bipartite. Indeed, edges require disjoint labels; on at most four indices, two such labels can be disjoint only when they are complementary two-element sets.

Color each \(S_i\) separately. Color a core vertex by its bipartition side together with the set of \(S_i\)'s it neighbors. This uses at most
\[
s+2\cdot2^s\leq36
\]
colors. It excludes monochromatic endpoints of length-three walks: a walk entirely in the core has opposite-side endpoints; if an internal vertex lies in some \(S_i\), equality of the endpoint signatures would produce a length-three walk between two vertices of \(S_i\).

From this coloring \(\phi\), construct a universal target with vertices
\[
(i,A),\qquad i\in[36],\quad A\subseteq[36]\setminus\{i\},
\]
and adjacency defined by
\[
(i,A)\sim(j,B)
\iff i\in B,\ j\in A,\ A\cap B=\varnothing.
\]
The map
\[
v\longmapsto\bigl(\phi(v),\{\phi(w):w\in N(v)\}\bigr)
\]
is a homomorphism. The length-three condition ensures disjoint neighbor-color sets across each edge. A triangle in the target is impossible: the first coordinate of its third vertex would belong to both sets attached to the other two vertices.

Thus the property holds for every \(c>1/5\), proving the upper bound on the infimum. This does not settle \(c=1/5\).

## Lower bound: dense obstructions for every \(c<1/9\)

For every finite triangle-free target \(H\), they construct an eligible graph not mapping to \(H\).

### High-chromatic seeds with nearly half-density independent covers

Let \(S(N,k)\) have increasing \(k\)-tuples as vertices, with consecutive overlapping windows adjacent. For fixed \(k\), its chromatic number is unbounded as \(N\) grows. A \(q\)-coloring induces a coloring of \(S(N,k-1)\) by sets of colors of right extensions, giving
\[
\chi(S(N,k-1))\leq2^{\chi(S(N,k))}.
\]
Iteration starts from \(S(N,1)=K_N\).

For even \(k\geq4\), each permutation of \([N]\) defines an independent set: select tuples whose permutation-largest entry occurs in position \(3,5,\ldots,k-1\). Adjacent windows cannot both qualify, because their common maximum shifts position by one. Counting all \(M=N!\) permutations, every vertex occurs in exactly
\[
r=M\frac{k-2}{2k}
\]
sets.

### Dense extension and obstruction

Orient the seed \(F=S(N,k)\), and replace each edge \(uv\) by
\[
u-x_{uv}-y_{uv}-v.
\]
Give these vertices types \(U,X,Y\), with labels \(u,u,v\), respectively.

For each type and each covering independent set, add \(W\) pads adjacent to precisely the base vertices of that type whose labels lie in that set. For each type, add another \(rW\) vertices, each adjacent to all \(MW\) pads of its family.

Writing \(b=|V(F)|+2|E(F)|\), the resulting graph satisfies
\[
n=b+3(M+r)W,\qquad \delta\geq rW.
\]

The crucial local lemma is that any length-three base walk with same-type endpoints has labels adjacent in \(F\). Therefore one pad cannot close such a walk into a five-cycle. Five-cycles with two pads would require an edge within one independent base type; cycles involving the added pad-only neighbors are excluded similarly. The base itself has girth at least nine. Triangles are also excluded by the type structure.

Choose \(\chi(F)>|V(H)|\). Any homomorphism to triangle-free \(H\) must send the original endpoints of every subdivided edge to different vertices: identifying them would create a closed three-walk in \(H\). Their images would therefore properly color \(F\), a contradiction.

Finally,
\[
\lim_{W\to\infty}\frac{rW}{n}
=\frac{k-2}{3(3k-2)}
\longrightarrow\frac19.
\]
For any \(c<1/9\), choose even \(k\) making this ratio exceed \(c\), then take
\[
W>\frac{cb}{r-3c(M+r)}.
\]
This disproves the property for every such \(c\).
